abstract: Chronotypes, often referred to in the context of sleep timing in humans (early/late sleepers) are heritable variations in timing of circadian behaviours. Chronotype differences among individuals have been associated with a myriad of psychological, metabolic, and physiological dysregulations. Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS) in humans have identified several circadian clock gene polymorphisms associated with divergent chronotypes; however, the lists of candidate genes vary across studies based on methodology and sampling strategy thus, necessitating more controlled studies on well-established model systems. Using long-term experimental evolution approach spanning over 20 years, we have derived a unique set of chronotypes in the form of 12 replicate Drosophila melanogaster populations that exhibit early/morning and late/evening emergence and have previously reported several circadian clock differences between the populations. We performed pooled DNA sequencing to explore genomic differences underlying early and late chronotypes and identified multiple genomic regions under selection. We observe that the early chronotype populations have primarily accumulated polymorphisms in genes related to photosensitivity, sleep, and the circadian clock, while the late chronotype populations have largely accumulated polymorphisms in genes related to the circadian clock, mRNA splicing mechanisms, and ecdysis. We further predict biological pathways under differential selection in the early and late chronotype populations. We believe these results provide evolutionary mechanisms behind chronotype divergence and will help generate verifiable hypothesis regarding target genes for phase divergence.
